Empirical Research Plan – Credit‐Supply Shock to Speculative-Grade Borrowers (1989-1990)

====================================================================
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension.

Rationale  
•  The junk-bond collapse was sudden, externally driven, and plausibly orthogonal to the operating performance of any single firm.  
•  Firms that relied on the speculative-grade bond market (rated BB+ or below prior to the shock) were disproportionately exposed.  
•  Investment-grade issuers faced the same macro-recession, tax law, and demand conditions but did not face a comparable contraction in their primary debt market.  
•  A DID comparing these two groups before vs. after 1989 therefore isolates the supply-driven component of financing conditions.  
•  Event-study (year-by-year leads/lags) is added to test for pre-trend violations and to trace dynamic effects.

====================================================================
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treatedi = 1 if firm i held a speculative-grade S&P long-term issuer rating (BB+ or lower) in 1988. Ratings are “frozen” at their 1988 value to avoid endogenous reclassification.

Control group  
Two alternative controls:  
a) Primary specification: firms rated investment-grade (BBB- and above) in 1988.  
b) Robustness: firms that were unrated in 1988 but had public equity listings (to test sensitivity).

Treatment timing  
Postt = 1 for fiscal years 1990–1993. Fiscal years 1986–1989 are the pre-period.  
(The Drexel bankruptcy was Feb-1990; FIRREA was Aug-1989. We drop 1989 as a transition year in a robustness check.)

Intensity variation (used in some specifications)  
JunkSharei = share of new debt issued through high-yield bonds during 1986-1988. This continuous measure allows difference-in-differences-in-continuous-treatment (Sun & Abraham 2021 style).

====================================================================
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the junk-bond shock, outcome trends for speculative- and investment-grade firms would have moved in parallel.  
Plausibility: Pre-1986–1988 trends in leverage, issuance, and investment appear similar in preliminary plots. We will formally test for differential linear trends.

A2. Rating exogeneity to the shock: 1988 credit ratings are determined before the supply contraction and are not affected by anticipation.  
Plausibility: The Drexel indictment (Mar-1989) and FIRREA (Aug-1989) were not widely anticipated in 1988; moreover, we use ratings as of 1988 (before the indictment).

A3. Stable composition/no selective attrition: Entry/exit or missing data does not differentially bias treated vs. control observations.  
Plausibility: Both groups have similar survivorship over a four-year window; we will verify attrition rates and use balanced-panel regressions as robustness.

A4. No spillovers across groups: Contraction in junk-bond supply does not mechanically reduce investment-grade supply (there is evidence of segmentation).  
Plausibility: Investment-grade volumes actually rose slightly in 1990–1991; nonetheless we will check for general-equilibrium price effects.

====================================================================
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Concurrent 1990–1991 macro recession.  
Mitigation: Year (or macro-variable) fixed effects absorb aggregate shocks common to both groups. Regional demand variation is also controlled for with Census-region × year FE.

T2. Banking capital crunch (regional, especially Northeast) could differentially hit certain treated firms.  
Mitigation: Add BankExposedi × Postt interaction (based on location in high-crunch states) to the regression; main results hold after netting this out (triple-diff). Also drop firms headquartered in the Northeast in a robustness test.

T3. Endogenous financing substitution induces mechanical changes in leverage ratios, complicating interpretation.  
Mitigation: Run separate equations for flows (issuance) and stocks (leverage). Use “flow-of-funds” decomposition: ΔLeverage = NetDebtIssuance − EquityIssuance − ChangeInAssets, which helps interpret causal channels.

====================================================================
5. R CODE OUTLINE
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast fixed-effects regressions
library(ggplot2)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
compu <- fread("compustat_1986_1993.csv")   # firm-year panel
# Assume 'rating' is S&P long-term issuer rating code (AAA=1 … D=…)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
compu[, treat_pre88 := as.integer(rating_1988 %in% c("BB+", "BB", "BB-", "B+", "B", "B-", "CCC+", "CCC", "CC", "C", "D"))]
compu[, control_pre88 := as.integer(rating_1988 %in% c("BBB-", "BBB", "BBB+", "A-", "A", "A+", "AA-", "AA", "AA+", "AAA"))]

# keep only obs belonging to either group
compu <- compu[(treat_pre88==1 | control_pre88==1)]

compu[, post := as.integer(year >= 1990)]
compu[, outcome_leverage := (lt + dlc)/at]             # book leverage example
compu[, outcome_netdebt := (dltis + dlcch - dltr)/at]  # net debt issuance / assets
compu[, firm_fe := gvkey]                              # id variable

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID regression
did_main <- feols(outcome_leverage ~ treat_pre88*post + 
                                  size + profitability + tangibility + mb +
                                  i(year) | gvkey,
                  data = compu, cluster = "gvkey")      # firm FE, year FE

summary(did_main)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study (leads/lags)
compu[, rel_year := year - 1989]   #  −3 … +4
event <- feols(outcome_leverage ~ i(rel_year, treat_pre88, ref = -1) + 
                                 size + profitability + tangibility + mb |
                                 gvkey + year,
               data = compu, cluster = "gvkey")

iplot(event)   # visual pre-trend check

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness – placebo shock in 1987
compu[, placebo_post := as.integer(year >= 1987)]
placebo <- feols(outcome_leverage ~ treat_pre88*placebo_post + 
                                 size + profitability + tangibility + mb |
                                 gvkey + year,
                 data = compu, cluster = "gvkey")
summary(placebo)
# Expect coefficient ~ 0 if parallel trends hold.
```

====================================================================
6. EXPECTED RESULTS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior expectations (relative to control, post-shock):  
•  Net debt issuance ↓ by ~2–3 % of assets per year for treated firms.  
•  Leverage ratio ↓ by ~3–5 p.p. (book) over 1990-1993.  
•  Firms substitute: bank loan share ↑ 1.5 p.p.; equity issuance ↑ 1–2 p.p.; trade credit ↑ slightly.  
•  Net investment (capex + acquisitions − asset sales) ↓ by 1–1.5 % of assets.  
•  Operating performance (ROA) falls modestly (≈0.5 p.p.) due to under-investment.

====================================================================
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0.5 = partly, 0 = doubtful)

C1. Parallel pre-trends documented .................................... 0.8  
C2. No compositional changes/attrition bias ........................... 0.7  
C3. Treatment exogeneity (no anticipation) ............................ 0.8  
C4. No spillovers / interference ...................................... 0.6  
C5. Robust standard errors & clustering appropriately ................. 1.0  

Overall credibility score ≈ 3.9 / 5.

====================================================================
End of Plan
